analytic.title: Energy-Efficient Task Scheduling and Synchronization for Multicore Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In the recent years, many energy-efficient realtime task scheduling algorithms have been proposed for multicore platforms. Most of them focus on independent tasks, however, relatively little work has been done in the presence of task synchronization. In this paper, we are interested in scheduling of real-time tasks which may make requests for accessing shared resources at the run time. A similarity-based task-to-core partitioning algorithm is proposed to allocate the tasks which may access a similar set of shared resources to the same core so that a large number of blockings can be avoided. Furthermore, we also propose speed assignment methods to assign proper processor speeds for tasks' executions with fullchip and per-core DVFS techniques so that the overall energy consumption can be reduced. The schedulability analysis of our proposed approach is provided in this paper. The capabilities of our proposed approach were evaluated by a series of experiments for which we have some encouraging results.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Nowadays, multicore processors have become the mainstream architecture for modern computer systems. Many excellent scheduling algorithms have been proposed to fully utilize the computing power from multiple cores such that high performance can be obtained. For saving more energy, most multicore processors also deployed with dynamic voltage/frequency scaling (DVFS) technique. When a processor (or a processing core) is not fully utilized, a simple strategy for saving energy is to slowdown the execution speeds of tasks so that the overall energy consumption can be reduced. However, such a strategy causes a significant impact on the performance since the lower execution speed delays in the completion of tasks. It brings a strong driving force in energy-efficient scheduling of real-time tasks because the late completion of a real-time task is allowed as long as it meets its timing requirements (such as deadline).

In the recent years, many excellent approaches have been proposed for energy-efficient real-time task scheduling on multicore processors with DVFS techniques. Most existing approaches assume that tasks are independent, however, relatively little work has been done for dependent tasks which is common in many real-life applications. When dependent tasks are considered, there are shared resources in the system and they have to be accessed in a mutual exclusive manner in order to maintain the data consistency. In this paper, we are interested in scheduling of dependent tasks for a realtime system with a multicore processor. A similarity-based task-to-core partitioning algorithm is proposed to assign the tasks which may access a similar set of shared resources to the same core so that a large number of blockings can be avoided. Tasks then are scheduled and synchronized by the well-known partitioned earliest deadline first (P-EDF) [1] and the multiprocessor stack resource policy (MSRP) [2]. Based on the schedulability analysis of P-EDF and MSRP, we also propose a speed assignment method to assign proper processor speed for tasks's executions so that the energy consumption can be reduced. Furthermore, we also propose a dynamic speed adjustment method to slowdown the processing speed whenever it is possible. The capabilities of our proposed approach were evaluated by a simulation platform, called MCRTsim [3], for which we have some encouraging results.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II summaries related work in the area of DVFS scheduling and synchronization for real-time systems with a uniprocessor or a multicore processor. Section III defines the system model and the problem. Section IV proposes our similaritybased partitioning algorithm with the schedulability analysis and the speed assignment/adjustement methods. Section V reports the performance evaluation. Section VI is the conclusion.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Energy-efficient scheduling of independent real-time tasks for uniprocessor environments have been studied extensively, a comprehensive survey can be found in [4]. Relatively little work has been done for dependent real-time tasks in the presence of task synchronization (such as [5][6][7]).

Similar with the development of the energy-efficient approaches for uniprocessor envrionments, the research for multicore environments also began with independent tasks scheduling (such as [8][9][10][11][12][13]). However, to the best of our knowledge, only limited work has been done for energyefficient synchronization of real-time systems in multicore environments (such as [14][15][16]). In particular, Han et al. [14] proposed a synchronization-aware worst-fit decreasing (SA-WFD) heuristic to partition tasks into clustered cores with the consideration on worst-case waiting time for accessing shared resources. Later, Saad et al. [15] extended SA-WFD to asymmetric multicore environment.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM DEFINITIONS
A. Multicore DVS Processors
div.p: We consider a multicore processor Π which consists of nc cores, i.e., Π = {core 1 , core 2 , • • • , core nc }, and it supports
div.formula: K discrete speeds S = {s 1 , s 2 , • • • , s K } where s min = s 1 < s 2 < . . . < s K = s max .
div.p: Without lose of generality, we assume the s max is 1 and all other speeds are normalized with respect to the maximum speed s max . We assume that Π supports full-chip and per-core DVFS capabilities. Let Speed i (t) be the operation speed of a core i at time t. We describe the full-chip and per-core DVFS as follows:

• full-chip DVFS: At the run time, all cores must be running at the same speed, i.e., Speed i (t) = Speed j (t) for any core i and core j ∈ Π at any time t. • per-core DVFS: At the run time, cores can be running at different speeds. In the rest of this paper, we use a function P C i (s) of the adopted speed s to represent the power consumption of a specified core i of Π. The energy consumption of the processor Π (including all cores) of an interval (t 1 , t 2 ] is defined as corei∈Π t2 t1 P C i (s(t)) dt, where s i (t) is the processor speed at time t.

div.head: B. Task and Resource Models
div.p: We consider a real-time system which consists of a set of n tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n }. Tasks are assumed to be periodic, preemptible, fixed-priority, and dependent due to concurrent accesses to shared resources. A task τ i is defined by a tuples (P i , A i , C i , T i , D i , Z i ), where P i is the priority, A i is the arrival time, C i is the worst-case computation amount, T i is the period, D i is the relative deadline of task τ i , and Z i is the list of τ i 's critical sections. Each task τ i is a template of its instances and each instance will arrive regularly for every period T i . Let τ i,j denote the jth instance of task τ i . The arrival time of τ i,j can be calculated by A i,j = A i + (j -1)T i . When a task τ i is executed at a processor speed s j , the worst-case execution time of τ i is Ci sj . Note that the worst-case execution time of the task could be C i if the task is executed at the maximum processor speed s max . A task instance τ i,j must be completed no later than its absolute deadline D i,j which is defined as its arrival time plus the relative deadline, i.e., D i,j = A i,j + D i . We consider well formed tasks which satisfy 0 ≤ C i ≤ D i ≤ T i , ∀τ i ∈ T . Note that we also assume that the relative deadline is equal to the period, i.e., D i = T i for every task τ i ∈ T .

In this paper, we are interested in scheduling and synchronization of real-time tasks with shared resources. We assume a set of m shared resources (e.g., shared variables, data objects, or files) R = {r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r m } can be accessed in the system. Shared resources do not allow to be accessed simultaneously. We assume that the access control of shared resources is guarded by semaphores to guarantee a mutual exclusion among the competing tasks. A piece of code that accesses a shared resource under mutual exclusion constraints is called a critical section. The critical sections of a task τ i is defined by a list Z i =< z i,1 , z i,2 , . . . , z i,ni >, where z i,j is the jth critical section of τ i . To maintain data consistency, a task must lock the corresponding semaphore before it enters a critical section and unlock the semaphore after the access of the critical section has been completed. We also assume that critical sections are properly nested. In particular, locks are released in the reverse order from which they were obtained.

div.head: C. Problem Definitions
div.p: Let lcm denote the least common multiple of all tasks' periods (also called hyperperiod). Since the task set T repeats an identical execution trace every hyperperiod, we only need to examine the time interval (0, lcm] for analyzing the performance and schedulability of the entire schedule [17]. The research problem is as follows:

Given a set of n real-time tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } and a set of m shared resources R = {r 1 , r 2 , • • • , r m }. The problem is to schedule T and to synchronize their accesses of R on a multicore DVFS processor Π which supports a set of
div.formula: K discrete speeds S = {s min = s 1 , s 2 , • • • , s K = s max }.
div.p: During a given time interval (0, lcm], this problem is to schedule T on Π and to decide the execution speed of tasks such that all tasks can meet their timing requirements (i.e., their deadlines) and the energy consumption
div.formula: corei∈Π t2 t1 P C i (s(t)) dt is minimized.
div.p: The problem is an optimization problem which is to find a feasible schedule which has minimal energy consumption. Note that a schedule is called feasible if all task instances in the schedule can be completed no later than their deadlines.

div.head: A. Task Scheduling
div.p: In this paper, we consider dynamic-priority-based approaches for the research problem because it can provide a higher utilization bound than that of fixed-priority task scheduling. In particular, we use the well-known partitioned earliest deadline first (P-EDF) [1] and multiprocessor stack resource policy (MSRP) [2] as the scheduling algorithm and the synchronization protocol. Under P-EDF, tasks are first partitioned among cores (i.e., tasks are assigned to cores) offline and then tasks are scheduled on the dedicated cores by EDF scheduling algorithm [17]. Note that the task partitioning is a N P-hard problem (it equals to the wellknown bin-packing problem). Several task mapping heuristics have been deployed for such a partitioning problem, such as worst-fit decreasing, first-fit decreasing, and best-fit decreasing. In the next subsection, we will propose a new partitioning method, called Similarity-Based Partitioning (SBP), to reduced energy consumption by partitioning tasks according to the similarity of their resource usages.

div.head: B. Similarity-Based Partitioning (SBP) Algorithm
div.p: The proposed similarity-based partitioning (SBP) algorithm is to partition tasks among cores by considering (1) the load balancing of multiple cores, and (2) the similarity of tasks' resource usages. Algorithm 1 shows the details of our proposed SBP algorithm. In particular, as shown in line 4, we first calculate an ideal utilization μ * = ( τi∈T Ci Ti )/nc, where nc is the number of cores. We then try to assign the tasks which have high similarity to the same core and the total utilization of the tasks cannot exceed μ * . The similarity of two task τ i and τ j is defined as ξ i,j which is calculated by |ResourceSet(τ i ) ∩ ResourceSet(τ j )|, as shown in lines 7-12. Let I be a set of the indices of all tasks, i.e., I = {1, 2, • • • , n}. Note that I is empty initially in line 5 and its elements are set in line 8. We also use a function asgned(τ i ) to indicate that τ i is assigned to a dedicated core or not. Initially, asgnCore(τ i ) is set as false for every task τ i , as shown in line 6.

Algorithm 1 uses two for loops to partition tasks into T 1 , T 2 , • • • , T nc according to the similarity of tasks. In the first loop, i.e., lines 13-34, we assign proper subsets of tasks to core 1 , core 2 , • • •, and core nc-1 . div.head: C. Task Synchronization
div.p: To ensure the data consistency of shared resources, we use MSRP to guarantee a mutual exclusion among the competing tasks from multiple cores. Under the MSRP, each task is assigned a fixed value, called preemption level, for predicting the potential blocking in the presence of dynamic-priority scheduling [2]. Let π i be the preemption level of a task τ i . The essential property of the preemption levels is that a task τ i can preempt another task τ j only if π i > π j . In this paper, the preemption levels of tasks are assigned inversely proportional to their relative deadlines (i.e., π i > π j ⇔ D i < D j ).

Since we use SBP algorithm to partition tasks among cores, a task τ i may access two types of shared resources: global and local resources. A global resource is accessed by tasks that assigned to different cores. A local resource is accessed only by tasks in the same core. When tasks are scheduled by P-EDF and MSRP, a task τ i is blocked if it attempts to access a global resource which has being locked by another lower-priority task on another core. Such a blocking is called remote blocking and the task must perform a busy waiting (also called spin lock) before it can gain the permission to access the global resource. In other words, the task has to wait (hold the processing core) until the global resource is released (i.e., unlock) by another task on another core. Furthermore, a task becomes non-preemptible when it is accessing a critical section for a global resource.
When local resources are considered, MSRP is the same as the SRP. For each local resource r l in core k , it is required to have a ceiling CL r l = max

div.p: ∅} which is the highest preemption level of all the tasks that may access to r j in core k . We also define a dynamic core ceiling CL * k (t) = max{{CL(r j )|r j is locked and currently being accessed} {∅}}. The dynamic core ceiling CL * k (t) is the highest ceiling of all the local resources that currently being accessed in core k at time t. Note that the core k 's dynamic core ceiling CL * k (t) is 0 when all core k 's local resources are free (i.e., unlocked) at time t, and it is updated whenever a core k 's local resource changes its state, i.e., be locked or unlocked by a task. When MSPR is adopted, a core k 's task τ i is not permitted to preempt the current task until (1) its priority is the highest among all ready tasks in core k , and (2) its preemption level is higher than core k 's dynamic core ceiling CL * k (t). When global resources are considered, we defined a global resource ceiling CL global k = max τi∈T k {π i } for each core k , which is the highest preemption level of all tasks that belong to the same core, i.e., core k . When a core k 's task τ i attempts to access a global resource r g , the following steps are performed: (1) the value of core k 's dynamic core ceiling CL * k (t) is raised to the value of CL global k , (2) the execution of τ i is set to be non-preemptible, and (3) check the state of the global resource r g . If r g is available (i.e., unlock), τ i locks r g successfully and enters its corresponding critical section to access r g . If r g is not available (i.e., locked by another task), τ i is added into r g 's waiting queue (a FCFS queue) and it uses busy waiting (i.e., spin lock) to wait until it gain the permission to use r g . Whenever a core k 's task τ i finishes its access to a global resource r g , the next waitingtask (from r g 's FCFS waiting queue) will continue to access r g until r g 's waiting queue is empty. After that, the core k 's global resource ceiling CL global will resume to its original value.

div.head: D. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: When tasks are scheduled to be executed on a uniprocessor, Baker [18] provided the following theorem:
div.formula: Theorem 1: (Baker[18]) A set of n real-time tasks is schedulable by EDF and SRP if ∀i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n, ( i k=1 C k T k ) + B i T i ≤ 1(1)
div.p: where B i is the worst-case blocking time of τ i . When multicore processors are considered, we have to discuss the interferences both from the local resources and the global resources. On one hand, let B l i be the worst-case blocking time of task τ i for accessing local resources. Under the MSRP, the value of B l i can be calculated by the following equations:
div.formula: B l i = m a x ∀zx,y∈Z l x ,τx∈T k -{τi} {|z x,y | : π x < π i , π i ≤ CL(R(z x,y ))}
div.p: (2) On the other hand, let B g i be the worst-case blocking time of task τ i for accessing global resources. The value of B g i can be calculated as follows:
div.formula: B g i = m a x zx,y∈Z g x ,τx∈T k -{τi} {|z x,y |+spin k (R(z x,y )) : π x < π i }
div.p: (3) where spin k (r g ) is the spin lock time (i.e., the busy waiting time) of r g in core k . Its value can be calculated as follows:
div.formula: spin k (r g ) = 1≤i≤nc,i =k max ∀zx,y∈Z g x ,τx∈T i {|z x,y | : R(z x,y ) = r g }(4)
div.p: Combine with Equation ( 2) and ( 3), the worst-case blocking time B i of task τ i can be obtained as the maximum of the B l i and B g i :
div.formula: B i = max{B l i , B g i } (5)
div.p: Furthermore, a task τ i have to paid an extra cost for spin lock (i.e., busy waiting) for waiting a global resource until it becomes available. We define spin k i be the worst-case spin lock time of task τ i for waiting a global resource in core k , which can be calculated as follows:
div.formula: spin k i = zx,y∈Z g i spin k (R(z x,y ))(6)
div.p: Based on the schedulability analysis of multiprocessor environments [2], the following theorem can be obtained:
Theorem 2: (Gai et al. [2]) A set of n real-time tasks is schedulable by P-EDF and MSRP if
div.formula: ∀k, 1 ≤ k ≤ nc, ∀τ i ∈ T k , i j=1 C j + spin k j T j + B j T j ≤ 1 (7)

div.head: E. Speed Assignment
div.p: The main objective of this subsection is to derive the execution speeds of tasks so that the energy consumption can be reduced without violating their timing constraints. In order to reach this goal, we will derive two approaches for two types of DVFS techniques, i.e., full-chip and per-core.

1) Apporaches for full-chip DVFS: When full-chip DVFS technique is adopted, we can calculate a base speed s base and use it to execute tasks so that the timing requirements of all tasks can be met. The calculation of s base is based on Equation (7):
div.formula: s base = min s * ∈S {s * : ∀k, 1 ≤ k ≤ nc, ∀τ i ∈ T k , i j=1 C j + spin k j T j + B j T j ≤ s * } (8)
div.p: 2) Approaches for per-core DVFS: When per-core DVS technique is adopted, we can also derive a base speed s base,k for each core k :
div.formula: s base,k = min s * ∈S {s * : ∀τ i ∈ T k , i j=1 C j + spin k j T j + B j T j ≤ s * } (9)
div.p: Note that we also propose a dynamic adjustment method to lower down the execution speed of a task whenever it is possible. Particularly, we can obtain the actual blocking time and the actual spin lock time at the time a task is starting its execution and the time a global resource is freed to be accessed. At these times, we can calculate a lower execution speed according to Equations ( 8) and ( 9) so that tasks can be executed with a lower energy consumption. Such a dynamic adjustment method is called dual speed for which a task is executed at a high speed (i.e., the base speed) initially and later switches to a low speed at the time its actual blocking time or the actual spin lock time is known. Note the a task instance τ i,j and other current executing tasks will be executed at the low speed until τ i,j 's deadline.

div.head: V. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: To better evaluate our proposed approach, we use a real-time scheduling simulator, called multi-core real-time scheduling simulator [3] to perform a series of experiments. By using MCRTsim, we evaluated a dual-core processor with the setting of its available processor speeds 100MHz to 1000MHz stepped by 100MHz and the corresponding power consumption 1.6W, 12.24W, 41.12W, 97.36W, 190.08W, 328.4W, 521.44W, 778.32W, 1108.16W, and 1520.08W. The testing task sets were generated with utilization settings from 0.2 to 1.8 Each task set contains 6-20 tasks randomly and the periods and worst-case computation amounts of tasks were selected from 100ms to 250ms and 8ms to 40ms randomly. We set the number of shared resources in the system is 4 to 8 to provide sufficient competition among tasks. The number of resources accessed by a task is selected randomly from 1 to 3. The position and the length of the critical sections within each task's execution were selected randomly. Note that the maximum length of any critical section z i,j was no larger than bf * C i , where bf is the blocking factor which specifies the maximum percentage of the blocking interval could occupy in a task's execution time. In our simulation, the value of bf was set to 0.3. The simulation time is 1,000,000ms (exclude the speed calculation overheads) and over 5 feasible task sets for each setting were evaluated in the experiments and their results were averaged.

These generated feasible tasks set were partitioned by our proposed SBP and worst-fit decreasing (WFD). When tasks have been partitioned by SBP or WFD, they were scheduled and synchronized by P-EDF and MSRP in MCRTsim. All task sets were evaluated under WFD and SBP for fullchip and per-core DVFS techniques labeled by fc and pc, respectively. We label the experimental results with base and dual when the tasks are executed at the base speed (i.e., s base or s base,k for full-chip and per-core DVFS) with and without the dynamic speed adjustment method. Furthermore, we also set a baseline for ease of comparison. The baseline approach is to partition tasks by WFD and always use the maximum speed s max for task executions. In our experiments, the primary performance metric of interest is the energy consumption of tasks, referred to as EnergyConsum, which can be calculated by experimental results were normalized with respect to the baseline.

Figures 1 and2 show the normalized energy consumption of the task set which has been executed on a dual-core processor. As we can see that the SBP outperforms WFD because SBP can reduce the number of remote blocking by partitioning tasks according to their similarity of the resource usages. Furthermore, the per-core outperforms full-chip in all cases. It is because the per-core has a better flexibility in using different execution speeds for different cores at the run time.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, a similarity-based task-to-core partition algorithm is proposed to assign dependent real-time tasks which may access a similar set of shared resources to the same core. We also proposed speed assignment methods for full-chip and per-core DVFS techniques to assign proper execution speeds for tasks. As the results, our proposed partition algorithm and speed assignment methods can reduce a large number of blockings so that the overall performance can be improved and the energy consumption can be reduced. The capabilities of our proposed approach were evaluated by MCRTsim for which we have some encouraging results.
